Field surveys of the armored catfish Hypostomus albopunctatus in the Paraná River basin indicate that individuals attain a maximum recorded total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], placing them among the larger-bodied members of the Loricariidae in this system. This ultimate size, which corresponds to a fully mature adult body, provides a useful benchmark for assessing growth trajectories across populations occupying different stream orders. Length-frequency distributions from seine-net collections consistently show that specimens exceeding this upper bound are exceptionally rare, suggesting that 40 cm represents a genuine physiological maximum rather than an artifact of sampling bias. This asymptotic length is also reflected in the calculated ultimate wet weight of 676.5 grams [Wwi = 676.5 grams], a mass that is consistent with the robust, heavily plated body architecture characteristic of this genus.

Sexual maturation in Hypostomus albopunctatus begins when individuals reach approximately 20 centimeters [Lp = approximately 20 centimeters] in total length, a size that corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence during the early wet season. This threshold was established through histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected monthly over two consecutive years, with the first appearance of vitellogenic oocytes or spermatogenic crypts used as the indicator of pubertal status. At this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty averages 82 grams [Wwp = 82 grams], a value that reflects substantial investment in somatic growth before reproductive effort commences. The size at maturity is relatively small compared to the ultimate total length, indicating a life-history strategy that partitions growth and reproduction across an extended adult phase. This pattern is typical among iteroparous loricariids inhabiting seasonally variable environments.

Reproductive output in this species has been estimated from fecundity dissections of gravid females collected during the peak spawning period at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Under those thermal conditions, final oocyte counts in ripe ovaries yield approximately 202 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 202 eggs per clutch], a moderate clutch size that is offset by a spawning frequency of about 12 clutches per year [F_R_i = about 12 clutches per year]. The resulting annual reproductive effort is considerable, reflecting a bet-hedging strategy in which females produce numerous eggs across multiple clutches across an extended breeding season. This pattern of repeated spawning is facilitated by group-synchronous ovarian development, with multiple cohorts of oocytes maturing sequentially. The daily egg production derived from these values is among the highest recorded for a loricariid of comparable body size.

Eggs of Hypostomus albopunctatus measure approximately 1 millimeter in diameter, and from this dimension the calculated wet weight at birth is 5.2e-4 grams [Wwb = 5.2e-4 grams], a remarkably low value that underscores the altricial, endotrophic state of the newly hatched larvae. Embryos develop within a protective adhesive chorion that secures the egg to submerged wood or rock surfaces in shallow, well-oxygenated riffles. When incubated at a stable temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], yolk-sac larvae emerge from the chorion after just 6 days [ab = 6 days], a brief developmental period typical of many loricariid species that spawn during warm, stable hydrological conditions. The newly emerged prolarvae remain attached to the substrate via cement glands on the head, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding approximately 48 hours after hatching.

Longevity estimates for Hypostomus albopunctatus derived from mark-recapture studies conducted at the same thermal regime of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C] indicate a maximum lifespan of 8 years [am = 8 years], with the oldest recaptured individual documented at 8 years post-hatching. This relatively extended lifespan for a medium-sized loricariid reflects the species' occupation of stable, low-predation habitats within the main channel and larger tributaries, where adult mortality from piscivorous fishes is comparatively low. The long reproductive window afforded by this lifespan allows females to accumulate substantial lifetime fecundity across many repeated spawning events, offsetting the per-clutch output. Comparative data from congeners inhabiting faster-flowing, higher-predation streams suggest that populations of H. albopunctatus in less disturbed reaches exhibit greater mean ages, consistent with a demographic response to reduced extrinsic mortality risk.
